page_title: REST Servers in Go: Part 2 - using a router package

summary.title: REST Servers in Go: Part 2 - using a router package
summary.one_liner: You learn how gorilla/mux simplifies method-based and parameterized routing in a Go REST server compared with hand-written routing in the standard library, and why the post notes that Go 1.22's enhanced mux makes this approach mostly obsolete.
keywords: how to route rest endpoints in go
takeaways: Hand-rolled routing in Go gets verbose quickly; a router package can centralize all route definitions in one place.
gorilla/mux lets you attach HTTP methods to routes and direct the same path to different handlers.
Regexp patterns in route paths distinguish /task/ from /task/<id>, and mux.Vars extracts named path parameters.
The post notes that since Go 1.22 the stdlib mux covers similar capabilities, so this approach is kept for historical reference.
summary.summary: The second part of a six-part-plus series on writing REST servers in Go revisits a task-tracker API and explains the routing problems that arise in no-dependency servers. It shows how gorilla/mux defines routes with per-method handlers, regexp-constrained path variables, and mux.Vars for extracting IDs, then compares the code-reading path against the hand-written version. The author argues a focused router package is a replaceable precision tool. A note at the top states that Go 1.22's enhanced stdlib routing makes this post largely outdated.
